cases.title: Blood pressure control with home telemonitoring
cases.context: In a clinical trial, adults with high blood pressure (hypertension) were randomly assigned to a home blood pressure telemonitoring program (a home cuff that sends each reading to a nurse) or to usual care. Blood pressure was counted as controlled when it was below 140/90 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) at 12 months. The table below shows the number of patients in each group whose blood pressure was controlled. A hospital newsletter reported the difference between the two groups "plus or minus" a margin of error.
tasks: (i) Calculate the proportion of patients whose blood pressure was controlled in each group and the difference, telemonitoring minus usual care.

(ii) What is the 95% margin of error for this difference? What is the 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of patients whose blood pressure was controlled between the two groups?

(iii) Using only your calculations for Parts (i) and (ii), is the difference in the proportion of patients whose blood pressure was controlled between these two groups statistically significant with \(P<0.05\)? Please state how you reached your conclusions.

hypotheses.nullWords: The proportion of patients with controlled blood pressure is the same with telemonitoring and with usual care.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The proportion of patients with controlled blood pressure is different with telemonitoring and with usual care.

cases.symbols: \(m_i\) (patients with the outcome), \(n_i\) (patients in the group), \(\hat p_i\) (sample proportion), \(\hat p\) (pooled proportion), \(s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}\) (SE of the difference), \(z_{0.05}\) (two-sided Normal cutoff), \(M\) (margin of error).

steps.title: Find both sample proportions
steps.words: Each proportion is the number of patients with the outcome divided by the number of patients in that group.

steps.title: Find the observed difference
steps.words: Keep the direction telemonitoring minus usual care in every later step.

steps.title: Pool the two groups
steps.words: Both groups are pooled to estimate one common proportion for the standard error, because the null hypothesis says the two proportions are equal.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the difference
steps.words: Multiply the pooled variance term by the sum of the reciprocal group sizes, then take the square root.

steps.title: Read the Normal cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, and use the infinity row in the 0.05 two-tail column. The infinity row is the standard Normal cutoff, 1.960.

steps.title: Calculate the margin of error
steps.words: This product is the number a report prints after "plus or minus".

steps.title: Form the interval and decide
steps.words: Zero lies outside the interval because the observed difference is larger than its margin of error, so reject equal proportions at the two-sided 0.05 level.

cases.conclusion: The telemonitoring minus usual care difference is 11.1 percentage points plus or minus 8.6 points (95% CI 0.0250 to 0.1970). The interval does not contain 0, so there is a difference (P < 0.05). A larger share of patients in the telemonitoring program had their blood pressure under control at 12 months.
cases.source: Original practice example in the course style

cases.title: Pressure ulcers on two ICU mattresses
cases.context: In a clinical trial, patients in an intensive care unit (ICU) were randomly assigned to an alternating-pressure air mattress (a mattress whose air cells inflate and deflate in turn) or to a standard foam mattress. The table below shows the number of patients in each group who developed a pressure ulcer (a skin wound caused by long pressure on the skin) within 14 days.
tasks: (i) Calculate the proportion of patients who developed a pressure ulcer in each group and the difference, alternating-pressure minus standard foam.

(ii) What is the 95% margin of error for this difference? What is the 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of patients who developed a pressure ulcer between the two mattress groups?

(iii) Using only your calculations for Parts (i) and (ii), is the difference in the proportion of patients who developed a pressure ulcer between these two groups statistically significant with \(P<0.05\)? Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.nullWords: The proportion of patients who develop a pressure ulcer is the same on both mattresses.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The proportion of patients who develop a pressure ulcer is different on the two mattresses.

cases.symbols: \(m_i\) (patients with the outcome), \(n_i\) (patients in the group), \(\hat p_i\) (sample proportion), \(\hat p\) (pooled proportion), \(s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}\) (SE of the difference), \(z_{0.05}\) (two-sided Normal cutoff), \(M\) (margin of error).

steps.title: Find both sample proportions
steps.words: Each proportion is the number of patients with the outcome divided by the number of patients in that group.

steps.title: Find the observed difference
steps.words: Keep the direction alternating-pressure minus standard foam. The difference is negative because fewer patients on the alternating-pressure mattress developed an ulcer.

steps.title: Pool the two groups
steps.words: Both groups are pooled to estimate one common proportion for the standard error, because the null hypothesis says the two proportions are equal.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the difference
steps.words: Multiply the pooled variance term by the sum of the reciprocal group sizes, then take the square root.

steps.title: Read the Normal cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, and use the infinity row in the 0.05 two-tail column. The infinity row is the standard Normal cutoff, 1.960.

steps.title: Calculate the margin of error
steps.words: This product is the number a report prints after "plus or minus".

steps.title: Form the interval and decide
steps.words: Zero lies inside the interval because the observed difference is smaller than its margin of error, so do not reject equal proportions at the two-sided 0.05 level.

cases.conclusion: The alternating-pressure minus standard foam difference is -5.1 percentage points plus or minus 8.8 points (95% CI -0.1390 to 0.0363). The interval contains 0, so there is no evidence of a difference (P > 0.05). In plain words, the share of ICU patients who got a pressure sore was about the same on the two mattresses, and the small gap seen in this trial could easily be due to chance.

cases.title: Community tai chi classes and 2-year deaths in older adults
cases.context: A study was reported concerning deaths among adults aged 75 years and older. Adults who chose to attend a weekly community tai chi class (a slow, low-impact exercise done standing) were compared with adults who did not attend a class. Deaths from any cause within 2 years were recorded. The adults decided for themselves whether to attend, so the groups were not formed by random assignment.
tasks: (i) Is there a difference in the 2-year death rate between the two groups? Use a chi-square test (with the Yates correction for the 2×2 table). State the hypotheses in words.
(ii) Calculate the relative risk of dying within 2 years, tai chi group relative to no-class group, and interpret it.
(iii) State what this comparison can and cannot show, given how the groups were formed.

hypotheses.nullWords: The 2-year death rate is the same for older adults who attend a tai chi class and for those who do not.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The 2-year death rate is different for older adults who attend a tai chi class and for those who do not.

cases.symbols: \(n_{TD}\) (deaths in the tai chi group), \(n_T\) (tai chi group size), \(n_{CD}\) (deaths in the no-class group), \(n_C\) (no-class group size), \(O\) (observed count), \(E\) (expected count), \(RR\) (relative risk).

steps.title: Find the group totals
steps.words: Add deaths and survivors in each row. The grand total is 4820 and the total number of deaths is 570.

steps.title: Calculate expected counts
steps.words: Expected counts are what each cell would hold if the death rate were the same in both groups.

steps.title: Calculate the Yates-corrected chi-square
steps.words: Subtract one half from each absolute discrepancy before squaring, because the table is 2×2.

steps.title: Compare with the chi-square cutoff
steps.words: Open Chi_Squared_Table1.pdf, page 1, row 1. The 0.05 column gives 3.841, the 0.005 column gives 7.879 and the 0.001 column gives 10.828. The statistic is larger than 7.879 but smaller than 10.828, so reject the null hypothesis with 0.001 < P < 0.005.

steps.title: Calculate both death proportions
steps.words: Each proportion is the risk of dying within 2 years in that group.

steps.title: Calculate the relative risk
steps.words: The risk of dying within 2 years in the tai chi group is about 75% of the risk in the no-class group.

steps.title: State what the design allows
steps.words: The adults chose whether to attend and were not assigned at random, so the result shows an association only. Adults who choose to attend an exercise class may be healthier or more mobile to begin with, so the lower death rate cannot be credited to tai chi itself. A randomized trial would be needed to show cause and effect.

cases.conclusion: Reject the null hypothesis (chi-square = 8.245, 1 df, 0.001 < P < 0.005). There is a difference in the 2-year death rate between the two groups. The relative risk is 0.7537, so the risk of dying within 2 years for an adult in the tai chi group is about 75% of the risk for an adult with no class. The adults chose for themselves, so this shows an association only and cannot show that tai chi lowers the risk.
cases.source: Original practice example in the course style

cases.title: Cardiac index on age in adults with and without heart failure
cases.context: In a study looking at heart function and age, cardiac index (the volume of blood the heart pumps each minute divided by body surface area) was measured at rest in liters per minute per square meter (L/min/m²) by echocardiography (ultrasound imaging of the heart) in 22 adults with heart failure (a heart that pumps too weakly for the body's needs) and 23 adults with no heart disease. Age was recorded in years. Separate R regressions of cardiac index on age were run for the two groups (subscript H for heart failure and N for no heart disease in the R names), and the summaries are shown below.
tasks: (i) State the null and alternative hypotheses for equal slopes in symbols and in words.
(ii) Calculate the standard error of the slope difference and the t statistic.

(iii) Is the relationship between cardiac index and age for adults with heart failure different than that for adults with no heart disease? Give the degrees of freedom, the critical value from the printed t table and the P range.

hypotheses.nullWords: Mean cardiac index falls with age at the same rate in adults with heart failure and in adults with no heart disease.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The rate at which mean cardiac index falls with age is different in adults with heart failure and in adults with no heart disease.

cases.symbols: \(b_1, b_2\) (sample slopes for the heart failure and no heart disease groups), \(s_{b_1}, s_{b_2}\) (slope standard errors), \(s_{b_1-b_2}\) (SE of the slope difference), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Read both slopes and standard errors
steps.words: Take the Age.H and Age.N rows of the two R coefficient tables, the Estimate column and the Std. Error column.

steps.title: Calculate the slope difference
steps.words: In these samples the slope for the heart failure group is steeper by about 0.022 L/min/m² per year of age, so the difference is negative.

steps.title: Calculate the SE of the difference
steps.words: The two samples are independent, so the variances of the two slopes add.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: Divide the slope difference by its standard error.

steps.title: Find df and the critical value
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1. There is no row 41, so use the printed row 40 above it, two-tail 0.05 column, which gives 2.021. A smaller df row has a larger cutoff, so this choice is conservative. Four degrees of freedom are lost because each line estimates an intercept and a slope.

steps.title: Decide and bracket P
steps.words: The magnitude of t is larger than the 0.05 cutoff but smaller than the 0.02 cutoff of 2.423, so 0.02 < P < 0.05. Reject equal slopes.

cases.conclusion: Reject equal slopes (t = -2.306, 41 df, 0.02 < P < 0.05 using the printed row 40). The relationship between cardiac index and age is different for adults with heart failure. Mean cardiac index is lower by about 0.046 L/min/m² per year of age in the heart failure group and by about 0.024 L/min/m² per year in the no heart disease group.

cases.title: Pulse oximeter readings on arterial saturation for two sensors
cases.context: Researchers interested in the accuracy of pulse oximeters (clip-on sensors that estimate blood oxygen saturation from light passing through a finger) did a study comparing two sensor models. In each patient, the oximeter reading (SpO2, in percent) was recorded at the same time as the arterial oxygen saturation measured on a blood sample by a blood gas analyzer (SaO2, in percent). Sensor model A was tested in 15 patients and sensor model B in 14 different patients. Separate R regressions of SpO2 on SaO2 were run for the two sensor models, and the summaries are shown below.
tasks: (i) State the null and alternative hypotheses for equal slopes in symbols and in words.
(ii) Calculate the standard error of the slope difference and the t statistic.
(iii) Is the relationship between SpO2 and SaO2 for sensor model A different than that for sensor model B? Give the degrees of freedom, the critical value from the printed t table and the P range.

hypotheses.nullWords: The mean oximeter reading rises with arterial saturation at the same rate for both sensor models.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The rate at which the mean oximeter reading rises with arterial saturation is different for the two sensor models.

cases.symbols: \(b_A, b_B\) (sample slopes), \(s_{b_A}, s_{b_B}\) (slope standard errors), \(s_{b_A-b_B}\) (SE of the slope difference), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Read both slopes and standard errors
steps.words: Take the SaO2.A and SaO2.B rows of the two R coefficient tables, the Estimate column and the Std. Error column.

steps.title: Calculate the slope difference
steps.words: Sensor A's reading rises about 0.066 percentage points more per point of arterial saturation than sensor B's in these samples.

steps.title: Calculate the SE of the difference
steps.words: The two samples are independent, so the variances of the two slopes add.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: Divide the slope difference by its standard error.

steps.title: Find df and the critical value
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 25, two-tail 0.05 column, which gives 2.060. Four degrees of freedom are lost because each line estimates an intercept and a slope.

steps.title: Decide and bracket P
steps.words: The magnitude of t is smaller than the 0.05 cutoff, so do not reject equal slopes. It lies between the 0.50 and 0.20 columns, so 0.20 < P < 0.50.

cases.conclusion: Do not reject equal slopes (t = 1.046, 25 df, 0.20 < P < 0.50). There is no evidence that the relationship between SpO2 and SaO2 is different for the two sensor models. Both slopes are close to 1 (0.947 and 0.880).

cases.title: Fluid intake on air temperature and years outdoors, least squares by matrix
cases.context: The table below shows data on daily fluid intake for 12 construction workers during a summer heat wave. Fluid intake (everything the worker drank during one working day) was recorded in milliliters (mL), the maximum air temperature on that day in degrees Celsius (°C), and the number of years the worker had worked outdoors. Fluid intake (y) is the dependent variable; maximum temperature (x1) and years outdoors (x2) are the independent variables.
cases.unit: mL per °C and mL per year
tasks: (i) Build \(X^TX\) and \(X^Ty\) from the sums of the data.
(ii) Solve \(b=(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty\) for \(b_0, b_1, b_2\) and provide the final regression line equation.
(iii) Use \(SS_{res}\) to find \(s_{y|x}\) and \(R^2\).
cases.symbols: \(X\) (design matrix, a column of ones, then x1 and x2), \(y\) (fluid intake vector), \(b\) (coefficient vector), \(SS_{res}\) (sum of squared residuals), \(SS_{tot}\) (total sum of squares), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(s_{y|x}\) (residual standard error).

steps.title: Build the cross-product matrix
general: X^TX=\begin{bmatrix}n&\sum x_1&\sum x_2\\\sum x_1&\sum x_1^2&\sum x_1x_2\\\sum x_2&\sum x_1x_2&\sum x_2^2\end{bmatrix}
steps.words: Each entry is a sum over the 12 workers. The first row and column come from the column of ones in X.

steps.title: Build the cross-product vector
steps.words: Multiply each column of X by the fluid intakes and add.

steps.title: Invert the cross-product matrix
steps.words: The inverse is found with software. Its diagonal entries are reused later for the coefficient standard errors.

steps.title: Solve for the coefficients
steps.words: These match the Estimate column of lm() in R, which prints -2710.89, 156.09 and 12.65.

steps.title: Calculate the residual variance
steps.words: Three parameters are estimated, so 9 degrees of freedom remain. The square root is the Residual standard error that R prints as 156.6.

steps.title: Calculate R squared
steps.words: About 83% of the variation in fluid intake is accounted for by maximum temperature and years outdoors together. R prints Multiple R-squared 0.8337.

cases.conclusion: The least-squares plane is ŷ = -2710.89 + 156.09x1 + 12.65x2 (mL), with s_y|x = 156.6 mL on 9 df and R² = 0.8337. Each extra degree of maximum temperature goes with about 156 mL more fluid intake when years outdoors is held fixed.
cases.source: Original practice example in the course style

cases.title: Serum ferritin with summary, confint, refit and prediction
cases.context: A study was reported concerning serum ferritin (a blood protein that stores iron) in 30 adults at a workplace health screening. Serum ferritin ("Ferritin"; nanograms per milliliter, ng/mL) is the dependent variable; age ("Age"; years), body mass index ("BMI"; kilograms per square meter, kg/m²) and resting heart rate ("HR"; beats per minute) are the independent variables. We are interested in investigating if these measures can "explain" serum ferritin. A multiple linear regression was run in R, and the code and output are shown below.
tasks: a) Using the R output, provide the final regression line equation.

b) Based on your R results, show how you would reject the null hypothesis of no relation between serum ferritin and all of the variables above (i.e., the null hypothesis that all of the coefficients are zero). Provide the alternate hypothesis as part of your answer.

c) Based on your R results, which explanatory variables are statistically significant? Provide the null and alternate hypotheses you are testing and summarize the test using the R results for each variable.

d) Using the confint() output, provide a 95% confidence interval for each of the three coefficients. Based on these confidence intervals, make an inference about the significance of each explanatory variable. Do these results agree with your conclusions in Part (c)?

If not all of the explanatory variables had statistically significant coefficients, re-do your analysis with only those that were statistically significant. Using the resulting regression equation (or your original equation, if all coefficients were statistically significant), estimate the serum ferritin of a person who is 58 years old, has a BMI of 29.5 kg/m², and has a resting heart rate of 72 beats per minute. You can do this later calculation by-hand.

hypotheses.nullWords: Resting heart rate has no relation to mean ferritin once age and BMI are in the model.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Resting heart rate is related to mean ferritin once age and BMI are in the model.

cases.symbols: \(b_j\) (coefficient estimate), \(s_{b_j}\) (standard error), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(\nu=n-k-1\) (residual degrees of freedom), \(\hat y\) (predicted mean ferritin).

steps.title: Write the full equation
steps.words: Read the Estimate column of the full summary. The result is a mean serum ferritin in ng/mL.

steps.title: Test the model as a whole
steps.words: Open F_table.pdf, page 1, numerator column 3, denominator row 26. The lightface value is 2.98 and the boldface value is 4.64. F is larger than both, so reject the null hypothesis that all three coefficients are zero (P < 0.01). R prints P = 7.184e-07.

steps.title: Test each coefficient
steps.words: Compare each magnitude with t_0.05(26) = 2.056 from t_table.pdf, page 1, row 26. Age is larger than 3.707, the 0.001 cutoff, so P < 0.001. BMI lies between 2.779 (0.01) and 3.067 (0.005), so 0.005 < P < 0.01. HR is smaller than 2.056, so HR is not significant (R prints P = 0.55633). The hand t for Age is 4.970 because it uses the rounded printed numbers, while R prints 4.972.

steps.title: Confirm with the 95% intervals
steps.words: The by-hand HR interval matches confint() to rounding. It contains 0, while the Age and BMI intervals do not, so the intervals agree with the t tests in Part (c).

steps.title: Refit without HR
steps.words: HR was not significant, so the model is refitted with Age and BMI only. The coefficients change a little because HR no longer shares the explanation. Both refit t values (5.038 and 3.701 on 27 df) are larger than 3.690, the 0.001 cutoff in row 27, so P < 0.001 for each.

steps.title: Predict by hand
steps.words: Substitute age 58 and BMI 29.5 into the refit equation. The heart rate of 72 beats/min is not used because HR is no longer in the model.

cases.conclusion: The model as a whole is significant (F = 19.69 on 3 and 26 df, P < 0.01), so at least one variable is related to ferritin. Age (P < 0.001) and BMI (0.005 < P < 0.01) are significant, but resting heart rate is not (t = -0.596, and its interval contains 0). The refit gives ŷ = 68.2863 + 0.6512·Age + 1.3800·BMI, and the estimated mean serum ferritin for a 58-year-old with a BMI of 29.5 kg/m² is 146.8 ng/mL.
cases.source: Original practice example in the course style
rOutput: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
Residual standard error: 8.003 on 26 degrees of freedom
Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
Residual standard error: 7.907 on 27 degrees of freedom
cases.rCode:
model <- lm(Ferritin ~ Age + BMI + HR)
summary(model)
confint(model)
model2 <- lm(Ferritin ~ Age + BMI)
summary(model2)

cases.title: Reading the R summary for serum ALT in fatty liver disease
cases.context: In a study looking at liver health, 40 adults with fatty liver disease (extra fat stored in the liver) had serum alanine aminotransferase (a liver enzyme that leaks into the blood when liver cells are damaged) measured after an overnight fast. Serum alanine aminotransferase ("ALT"; units per liter, U/L) is the dependent variable; waist circumference ("Waist"; centimeters, cm), physical activity ("Activity"; hours per week) and nightly sleep ("Sleep"; hours per night) are the independent variables. We are interested in investigating if these measures can "explain" serum ALT. A multiple linear regression was run in R, and the code and output are shown below.
tasks: a) Using the R output, provide the final regression line equation.

b) Based on your R results, show how you would reject the null hypothesis of no relation between serum ALT and all of the variables above (i.e., the null hypothesis that all of the coefficients are zero). Provide the alternate hypothesis as part of your answer.

c) Based on your R results, which explanatory variables are statistically significant? Provide the null and alternate hypotheses you are testing and summarize the test using the R results for each variable.

d) Using the confint() output, provide a 95% confidence interval for each of the three coefficients. Based on these confidence intervals, make an inference about the significance of each explanatory variable. Do these results agree with your conclusions in Part (c)?

If not all of the explanatory variables had statistically significant coefficients, re-do your analysis with only those that were statistically significant. Using the resulting regression equation (or your original equation, if all coefficients were statistically significant), estimate the serum ALT of an adult who has a waist circumference of 98 cm, does 3 hours of physical activity per week, and sleeps 6.5 hours per night. You can do this later calculation by-hand.

hypotheses.nullWords: None of waist circumference, physical activity and sleep is related to mean serum ALT.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: At least one of the three variables is related to mean serum ALT.

cases.symbols: \(R^2\) (multiple R-squared), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(n\) (number of adults), \(MS_{mod}, MS_{res}\) (model and residual mean squares), \(b_j\) (coefficient), \(s_{b_j}\) (its standard error).

steps.title: Find the F degrees of freedom
steps.words: Three independent variables are tested together, so 36 degrees of freedom remain for the residuals.

steps.title: Recompute F from R squared
steps.words: Dividing SS_mod and SS_res by SS_tot turns them into R² and 1 − R², so F can be checked from the printed R². R prints 14.07, and the small gap comes from the rounded R².

steps.title: Compare with the F cutoff
steps.words: Open F_table.pdf, page 2, numerator column 3, denominator row 36. The lightface value is 2.86 and the boldface value is 4.38. F is larger than both, so reject the null hypothesis that all three coefficients are zero with P < 0.01. R prints P = 3.166e-06.

steps.title: Test the waist coefficient
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 36. The 0.05 column gives 2.028. The statistic is also larger than 3.582, the 0.001 cutoff, so P < 0.001. R prints 3.03e-05.

steps.title: Test the activity coefficient
steps.words: The magnitude lies between 2.990 (0.005) and 3.333 (0.002), so 0.002 < P < 0.005. R prints 0.00219. More activity goes with lower ALT when the other two variables are held fixed.

steps.title: Test the sleep coefficient
steps.words: The magnitude lies between 2.028 (0.05) and 2.434 (0.02), so 0.02 < P < 0.05. R prints 0.02258. Sleep is significant at the 0.05 level but not at the 0.02 level.

steps.title: Build 95% intervals for the three slopes
steps.words: These match the confint() output to rounding, because R uses the exact cutoff 2.0281 for 36 df. No interval contains 0, which agrees with the three t tests. The Sleep interval ends close to 0, which matches its P value near 0.02.

steps.title: Predict by hand
steps.words: All three variables are significant, so the original equation is used. Substitute a waist of 98 cm, 3 hours of activity and 6.5 hours of sleep. The result is a mean serum ALT in U/L.

cases.conclusion: Reject the null hypothesis of no relation (F = 14.07 on 3 and 36 df, P < 0.01 from the printed table and P = 3.166e-06 from R). Waist (P < 0.001), Activity (0.002 < P < 0.005) and Sleep (0.02 < P < 0.05) are each significant, and no 95% interval contains 0. The fitted equation is ŷ = 74.07893 + 0.42808·Waist − 1.73852·Activity − 2.50532·Sleep, and the estimated mean serum ALT for the adult described is 94.5 U/L.
cases.source: Original practice example in the course style
rOutput: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
Residual standard error: 7.587 on 36 degrees of freedom
cases.rCode:
model <- lm(ALT ~ Waist + Activity + Sleep)
summary(model)
confint(model)

cases.title: Probability and odds of kidney injury after bypass surgery
cases.context: In a study looking at kidney injury after heart surgery, 80 patients were followed after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB, a heart-lung machine that pumps and oxygenates the blood during the operation). Acute kidney injury (AKI, a sudden fall in kidney function) in the week after surgery was recorded as present (1) or absent (0), and the time on bypass was recorded in minutes (min). R fit glm(AKI ~ CPB, family = "binomial") and printed the summary below.
tasks: (i) Based on the R results, is the probability of AKI related to the time on bypass? Use the z value for CPB.
(ii) Calculate the probability of AKI for a patient who was on bypass for 150 min.
(iii) Calculate the odds of AKI at 150 min and state them as odds to 1.

hypotheses.nullWords: The probability of AKI does not change with the time on bypass.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The probability of AKI changes with the time on bypass.

cases.symbols: \(b_0, b_1\) (maximum-likelihood estimates), \(x\) (time on bypass, min), \(p\) (probability of AKI), \(z\) (estimate divided by its standard error).

steps.title: Test the bypass time coefficient
steps.words: Use the infinity row of t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, for the Normal cutoffs. The 0.05 column gives 1.960 and the 0.001 column gives 3.2905. The statistic is larger than both, so reject with P < 0.001. R prints 0.000113.

steps.title: Form the linear predictor
steps.words: The linear predictor is the logit, the natural log of the odds of AKI.

steps.title: Convert to a probability
steps.words: The logistic function keeps the result between 0 and 1. Rounded to two places, p = 0.34.

steps.title: Calculate the odds
steps.words: Dividing the rounded probability 0.34 by 0.66 gives 0.515. Carrying p unrounded gives 0.508. The odds are below 1 because AKI is less likely than not at 150 min.

cases.conclusion: Time on bypass is a significant predictor of AKI (z = 3.860, P < 0.001). A patient with 150 min on bypass has an estimated AKI probability of 0.3371 (0.34), and odds of about 0.52 to 1 from the rounded probability (0.51 to 1 unrounded).
cases.source: Original practice example in the course style

cases.title: Stent restenosis and balloon inflation pressure
cases.context: Researchers interested in restenosis (renarrowing of an artery after it has been opened) did a study of 50 patients who received a coronary stent (a small mesh tube placed in a narrowed heart artery). The maximum balloon inflation pressure used to expand the stent was recorded in atmospheres (atm), and restenosis at 9 months was recorded as present (1) or absent (0). R fit glm(Restenosis ~ Pressure, family = "binomial") and printed the summary below.
tasks: (i) Based on the R results, is the probability of restenosis related to the inflation pressure?
(ii) Calculate the probability of restenosis at 10 atm and at 18 atm.
(iii) Calculate the factor by which the odds of restenosis change for each 1 atm increase.

hypotheses.nullWords: The probability of restenosis does not change with inflation pressure.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The probability of restenosis changes with inflation pressure.

cases.symbols: \(b_0, b_1\) (maximum-likelihood estimates), \(x\) (inflation pressure, atm), \(p\) (probability of restenosis), \(e^{b_1}\) (odds multiplier per atm).

steps.title: Test the pressure coefficient
steps.words: Use the infinity row of t_table.pdf, PDF page 2. The statistic is smaller than the 0.05 Normal cutoff 1.960, so do not reject. It lies between the 0.20 column (1.2816) and the 0.10 column (1.6449), so 0.10 < P < 0.20. R prints 0.1882. The hand z is 1.315 because it uses the rounded printed numbers, while R prints 1.316.

steps.title: Probability at 10 atm
steps.words: At the low end of the pressures used, the fitted probability of restenosis is about 0.14.

steps.title: Probability at 18 atm
steps.words: At a high pressure the fitted probability is about 0.32. The coefficient was not significant, so this gap between the two fitted values is not evidence that pressure changes the risk.

steps.title: Odds multiplier per atmosphere
steps.words: Each 1 atm increase multiplies the fitted odds of restenosis by about 1.141. The z test did not reject, so this factor is not significantly different from 1.

cases.conclusion: Do not reject the null hypothesis (z = 1.315, 0.10 < P < 0.20). There is no evidence that the probability of restenosis changes with inflation pressure. The fitted probabilities are 0.140 at 10 atm and 0.319 at 18 atm, and the fitted odds multiplier is 1.141 per atm, but neither is significantly different from no change.

notes: All data are invented for practice. The raw data behind every table and every R printout are stored in check_session19.py (DATA), which refits each model with NumPy/SciPy and compares every printed number.

Every R printout is real Rscript output (R 4.6.1) from those data, stored line for line in the case-level keys rOutput and rCode, the keys the neuroscience pack uses for summary(lm()) printouts. Only blank lines at the very start and end were trimmed. The `table` of each R case carries the same numbers in the reference layout (coefficient rows plus one summary row, and an Output column for the summary, confint and refit case).

As in the reference cases, by-hand values for the R cases use the printed (rounded) R numbers, so a few hand values differ from R in the last digit (t for Age 4.970 against 4.972 in p19-ferritin-screening-refit, z 1.315 against 1.316 in p19-stent-pressure-restenosis, F 14.06 against 14.07 in p19-fatty-liver-alt-summary). The step words say so.

p19-cardiac-index-age-slopes has 41 degrees of freedom. t_table.pdf has no row 41, so the solution uses the printed row 40 (2.021 at 0.05, 2.423 at 0.02), which is conservative. Its lookup is flagged approximation true with actualDf 41.

Outcome mix. Do not reject: p19-mattress-pressure-ulcer-margin (interval contains 0), p19-oximeter-sensor-slopes (t = 1.047), p19-stent-pressure-restenosis (z = 1.315), and the HR variable in p19-ferritin-screening-refit (dropped and the model refitted). Close to a cutoff: refit BMI t = 3.701 against the 0.001 cutoff 3.690 in row 27, and Sleep t = −2.383 between 2.028 and 2.434.

The slopes cases keep the reference value keys bM, sbM, nM (first group, heart failure or sensor A) and bF, sbF, nF (second group), while the symbols shown to the student are b_1, b_2 or b_A, b_B. The logistic cases keep the reference value keys because the logistic board reads them. In p19-bypass-time-kidney-injury, `age` holds the bypass time 150 min. In p19-stent-pressure-restenosis, `p53` and `p75` hold the probabilities at 10 and 18 atm, `oddsPerDegree` is the odds multiplier per atm and `halfwayTemp` is the pressure where the fitted probability is one half (23.7 atm, outside the data, so it is not used in the steps).

The R-summary cases carry the variable list in the homework's own form ("Name"; unit) and the homework's Part (a) to (d) wording plus the refit and prediction paragraph. These are the only semicolons in context and tasks. check_session19.py allows colons and semicolons in context and tasks only.

Both margin cases use proportions with the pooled standard error and the Normal cutoff, exactly as the reference margin case does, so the value keys match. The margin for a difference of two means (t cutoff times the SE) is not covered here.
